mappings.name: the stub's hosted payment page: a Pay link, a Cancel link, and the payer's window

file: GET /stub-hosted-page/{pay_token} -- what a payer's BROWSER sees after
vpay redirects them, standing in for Orange Money's own hosted page; the
two controls on it; and the WHOLE of the payer's state machine, which is
the WireMock scenario `orange-hosted-page-payer`.
webpayment.json has answered every accepted submit with a payment_url
under this path since Step 3, and until Step 9 nothing served it: a
payer following the URL vpay handed them got WireMock's 404. Step 9's
D7 makes it a page with two links, so a browser -- Cypress in
frontends/tests/e2e, or a human running `just demo` -- can finish the
redirect leg instead of stopping at the redirect.
ADR-0006 allows this: a stub rail is a WireMock HOST in configuration,
reached over HTTP exactly as the rail is. It is a stub of the RAIL's
page. It is not, and must never become, a stub of a vpay page --
vpay's own return page is frontends/apps/checkout's, served by vpay.
WHAT CHANGED ON 2026-09-10 (issue #58), AND WHY.
Until then this stub answered the FIRST transactionstatus SUCCESS, and
the demo's Orange test numbers therefore did not work from a browser:
`vpay_api::v1::payment_intents`'s confirm handler enqueues the
`poll_charge` job with `run_at = now()` -- `poll_delay(0)` is the delay
before the SECOND attempt, not the first -- and `vpay_worker`'s idle
sleep is one second. Measured on the demo stack on 2026-09-06 from this
container's own request journal: webpayment at T, the payer landing on
this page at T+44 ms, the first transactionstatus at T+449 ms, the
payer's form at T+11.96 s. The order came back PAID for 237600000400.
So the payer now has a WINDOW, and it is bounded at both ends:
submit           -> `submitted`          (webpayment.json arms it)
1st status       -> PENDING              -> `submitted-polled`
2nd status       -> SUCCESS (catch-all)  -> `Started`
... unless a payer lands on this page, which at any point arms the
bounded chain instead:
GET this page    -> `payer-on-page-1`
status x4        -> PENDING              -> `payer-never-acted`
status           -> EXPIRED              -> `Started`
... and each of the page's three exits arms a terminal answer:
#pay / the form  -> `payer-paid`         -> SUCCESS, then `Started`
#cancel          -> `payer-gave-up`      -> EXPIRED, then `Started`
the form + a test number -> demo-outcomes.json's two arms
THE FIRST RUNG IS UNCONDITIONAL, AND THAT IS THE POINT. Arming only on
this page's GET would be a RACE: the browser's GET and the worker's
first poll are 44 ms and 449 ms out of the same submit, and which lands
first depends on where in its one-second idle sleep the worker happened
to be. One PENDING answer that depends on nothing but the submit turns a
~400 ms margin into a ~10 s one (the first rung of `poll_delay`), which
is what makes `shop-hosted.cy.ts`'s Orange legs deterministic rather
than usually-green. It costs the Orange happy path one rung, and it
costs the merchant demo nothing at all: those two mappings sit at
priority 6, BELOW demo-outcomes.json's amount-keyed mappings (4), so
5001 and 5002 are still terminal on the first rung.
PRIORITIES, and why each is what it is. Lower wins.
1  transactionstatus.json's order_id-keyed cases. The conformance
suite depends on them and they must keep winning: a case that
submits and then asks about REF_SLOW is asking about REF_SLOW.
3  every mapping below that answers from a payer's PRESENCE or ACTION.
Above the amount-keyed demo mappings (4) deliberately: a payer
standing on this page is the strongest statement about a charge
that this stub can have, and settling it from the amount while they
are still reading is the bug this file exists to fix.
4  demo-outcomes.json's amount-keyed mappings -- the HEADLESS demo
(`just demo-walk`), which opens no browser and never GETs this page.
6  the two unconditional rungs above. Below 4 on purpose.
10 transactionstatus.json's catch-all SUCCESS.
STRICTLY SEQUENTIAL. One scenario per container, so two Orange charges
in flight against one stub share it and the wrong one could be answered.
Every one of the mappings below either transitions to `Started` or is
re-armed by the next submit, so no charge inherits a state nobody chose;
what is not fixable in WireMock is two charges overlapping. The demo and
both Cypress specs drive one payment at a time.
Commentary lives in `metadata` because WireMock fails to start on a
mapping document containing any field it does not recognise.
comment: WHY THE LINKS COME OUT OF THE QUERY STRING, AND WHY THE REAL RAIL DOES
NOT WORK THIS WAY.
Orange's real page is stateful: the submit hands the rail return_url and
cancel_url, the rail STORES them against the pay_token, and the page it
later serves at that token renders them from its own database. The payer
never sees those URLs in the address bar of the page they are sent to.
WireMock cannot do that. Response templating renders from the CURRENT
request only: {{request.*}} is this GET, and there is no handlebars
helper that reaches into the request journal for the POST that minted
the token. A stateful stub would need a scenario per token (there is one
per charge, generated at runtime) or a postServeAction that wrote a new
mapping (a plugin this image does not carry, and a stub that rewrites
itself while a suite is running).
So the token is carried WITH its two URLs: webpayment.json's response
templates payment_url as
/stub-hosted-page/{pay_token}?return=<urlEncoded>&cancel=<urlEncoded>
and this mapping carries them straight back out -- on the form's hidden
inputs, and, since 2026-09-10, on the two links as well. The pairing is
preserved -- these are the exact bytes THAT submit carried, not a
deployment-wide constant -- which is the property a test of the return
trip needs. What is lost is the rail-side storage, and with it any claim
that Orange would accept a return_url it had not been told about at
submit. Nothing in this repository makes that claim.
THE LINKS NOW GO THROUGH THIS CONTAINER, and that is the change issue
#58 asked for. Until 2026-09-10 `#pay` and `#cancel` pointed STRAIGHT at
the return URL, so a payer who used them never touched this stub again --
which is exactly why exp22 could not close the race: there was no way to
learn that a payer had acted. They now point at /pay and /cancel on this
container, which 302 to the same two URLs. The redirect is what a test
asserts on, and it is a STRONGER assertion than the old href one: the
bytes are not merely rendered into a page, they are the Location a payer's
browser is actually sent to.
TRIPLE STACHE, {{{...}}}, not double, on everything that is a URL -- and
MEASURED, on 2026-09-10, rather than reasoned about, because the reasoning
this file used to carry was wrong.
What it used to say: that the double stache HTML-escapes, so the hidden
inputs below could be written with it and a `&` would reach the browser as
`&` and be read back as `&`. That is Handlebars' documented behaviour
and it is NOT this image's. Driven against wiremock/wiremock:3.9.2 with a
return URL of `https://m.test/back?q="x"&y=<z>`, the rendered page carries
<input type="hidden" name="return" value="https://m.test/back?q="x"&y=<z>">
-- unescaped, quotes and all, which closes the attribute early. So the
double stache is not protecting anything, and the choice between the two
staches changes nothing at all for a value with no HTML metacharacters in
it. It is left as the double stache only because changing it would be a
diff that fixes nothing.
The two HREFS are a different matter and are safe, because they do not rely
on the stache: they wrap the URL in WireMock's `urlEncode` helper first, so
what lands in the attribute is percent-encoded and contains no `"`, `<` or
`&` at all. The literal separator between this container's own two query
parameters is written `&` because it is inside an attribute, and that
one IS a literal in the template rather than something a stache produced.
WHAT IS STILL BROKEN, AND IS NOT THIS CHANGE'S TO FIX: a return_url
containing a double quote would break the FORM below, because a GET form's
hidden input has to carry the DECODED value (the browser percent-encodes it
again on submit) and WireMock cannot HTML-escape an attribute. The links
are immune; the form is not. No test in this repository sends such a URL,
and `vpay_api`'s `checked_return_url` is what would have to refuse one.
The urlPathPattern is loose on the token because it is generated per
charge: pay-<uuid> from the catch-all, pay-dup-1 from the duplicate
scenario. Nothing here reads it -- it is in the path so a captured
request says which charge a payer was looking at.
Proven by the_stub_hosted_page_links_to_the_return_url_the_submit_carried
in backends/tests/integration/tests/confirm_rails.rs, which confirms a
real intent, follows the payment_url the rail answered with, and then
follows both of the page's links and asserts each 302 lands on the
merchant's own return URL.

response.body:
Orange Money — page de paiement (stub)

This page is a WireMock stub of the rail's hosted page. It is not Orange, it moves no money, and it decides nothing: the outcome of this charge comes from vpay's authenticated status query.

Reference: {{request.pathSegments.[1]}}

While you are on this page the rail answers vpay's status query PENDING, for a bounded number of polls. Choose one of the two links below, or pay with a test number; do nothing for long enough and the page expires.

Pay Cancel

Or pay with one of the demo's test numbers

Orange is a redirect rail: the number is typed here, on the rail's own page, and vpay never sees it. That is why the demo steers this rail's outcome from this form rather than from anything the merchant sent. The numbers are documented in examples/shop/README.md; anything not listed there pays.

mappings.name: a submitted charge nobody has looked at yet is PENDING once

why: THE RUNG THAT REMOVES THE RACE. `submitted` is armed by
webpayment.json's accepted submit -- by the charge existing, not by
anything a payer did -- so this answer does not depend on whether the
payer's browser has reached the hosted page yet. It buys the whole
first rung of `vpay_worker::poll_delay` (10 s) for that GET to land
in, against the ~400 ms it had before.
PRIORITY 6: below demo-outcomes.json's amount-keyed mappings (4), so
`just demo-walk`'s 5001 and 5002 outcomes are still answered
terminally on the first rung and that program's timings do not move;
above transactionstatus.json's catch-all SUCCESS (10), which is the
answer this defers by one rung.
It is also the only mapping in this scenario a charge reaches with no
payer involved at all, which is why it hands over to a state that
falls straight back to the catch-all rather than to more PENDING: a
charge nobody is paying must still settle the way it always did.

mappings.name: and settles on the next ask, exactly as it did before the window existed

why: The same body transactionstatus.json's priority-10 catch-all serves,
one rung later, and a transition back to `Started` so the next charge
on this container inherits nothing. Written out here rather than left
to fall through because falling through would leave the scenario in
`submitted-polled` for ever.
PRIORITY 6, for the reason the mapping above gives: 5001 and 5002 are
answered by demo-outcomes.json (4) whatever this scenario's state is.

mappings.name: a payer is on the page: PENDING (1 of 4)

why: Poll 1 of 4 while a payer is on the page.
WHY 4 AND NOT SOME OTHER NUMBER. The chain has to be
long enough that a payer can read the page and click, and short
enough that a charge nobody pays still reaches a terminal state.
`vpay_worker::poll_delay` is 10s, 20s, 30s, 45s, 60s, 90s, then
120s, so 4 PENDING answers put the terminal one at
10+20+30+45 = 105 seconds after the payer landed -- comfortably
over the 30 seconds issue #58 asks for, and comfortably under the
two-minute outcome timeout the Cypress specs give a charge.
That arithmetic is not a comment: `the_pending_chain_gives_a_payer
_at_least_thirty_seconds_on_the_worker_s_own_ladder` in
backends/tests/integration reads THIS FILE and `poll_delay` and
fails if either moves under the other.
PRIORITY 3 on every rung: above demo-outcomes.json's amount-keyed
mappings (4), because a payer who is standing on the rail's page
is a stronger statement about a charge than the amount a merchant
chose; below transactionstatus.json's order_id-keyed cases (1),
which the conformance suite depends on.

mappings.name: a payer is on the page: PENDING (2 of 4)

why: Poll 2 of 4 while a payer is on the page.

mappings.name: a payer is on the page: PENDING (3 of 4)

why: Poll 3 of 4 while a payer is on the page.

mappings.name: a payer is on the page: PENDING (4 of 4)

why: Poll 4 of 4 while a payer is on the page.

mappings.name: the payer never acted: the page expires

why: The chain's terminal answer, and the reason the chain is BOUNDED. A
payer who leaves the tab open must not leave a charge polling PENDING
for the twenty-four hours `docs/flows/reconciler.md` gives the ladder.
EXPIRED -> payer_timeout (vpay_adapter_orange_money::mapping::
STATUS_TABLE, docs/flows/adapter-orange-money.md): 'the payer never
entered the one-time code before the hosted page aged out' is
precisely what has happened here.
Answered ONCE and then disarmed, for the reason MTN's file gives:
EXPIRED is terminal, the worker settles on it and asks nothing more,
and leaving the scenario armed would make the NEXT charge inherit an
outcome nobody chose.

mappings.name: the payer paid: the #pay link, and the form with any number the demo does not steer

why: The success exit, and the DISARM. Priority 5 so demo-outcomes.json's
two number-keyed arms (3) win when the payer typed one of those; this
one carries every other number, and the `#pay` link, which carries no
`msisdn` parameter at all.
302 to the return URL THIS submit carried, taken out of the query
string the page put on the link (or out of the form's hidden input,
which holds the same bytes). Not followed by the conformance suite's
client -- `vpay_provider::http::client` refuses redirects on purpose --
so the Location is directly assertable.

mappings.name: the armed payment answers SUCCESS once, then disarms

why: What the payer's click is FOR. Without it the click would only
disarm the chain and the charge would settle on the catch-all anyway,
one rung later -- which is the same answer for the wrong reason, and
would leave `the_payer_who_clicks_pay_settles_the_charge` passing for
a stub that had never noticed the click. This mapping is what the
'drop the click arming' mutation deletes.
PRIORITY 3, with the rest of the payer's own actions.

mappings.name: the payer gave up: the #cancel link

why: The abandon exit. 302 to the CANCEL url this submit carried -- which
`vpay-adapter-orange-money` fills with the charge's single return_url,
because Orange's page distinguishes paid from cancelled and vpay
cannot (docs/flows/adapter-orange-money.md). Two URLs, one value, and
this mapping reads the one the page's #cancel link carried so that a
deployment which ever DID send two would land the payer on the right
one without this file changing.
ORANGE HAS NO `CANCELLED` STATUS. Its five documented statuses are
INITIATED, PENDING, SUCCESS, EXPIRED and FAILED, so a stub answering
CANCELLED would be this repository inventing a rail vocabulary --
exactly what examples/shop/README.md refuses to do elsewhere. A payer
who abandons the page is a page that ages out unpaid, which is
EXPIRED, which is payer_timeout. That is also why this shares
`payer-gave-up` with nothing: it is its own state so a captured
journal says which exit a payer took.

mappings.name: the armed abandonment answers EXPIRED once, then disarms

why: EXPIRED -> payer_timeout, the same mapping the chain's own expiry
uses and for the same reason: the page ended without a payment.
Answered once and disarmed, because it is terminal.
